full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury J.-This appeal by way of special leave is directed against the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1479 of 1979 setting aside the order passed by the District Judge, Sylhet in Misc. Case No. 4 of 1979. 

 2. The plaintiff’s respondents filed SC.C. Suit No. 24 of 1976 for eviction of the appellant. The suit premises belonged to Rajani Kanta Singh, husband of the plaintiff No. 1, and father of the plaintiff’s respondents 2 to 4. Case of the plaintiffs was that the defendant appellant was a monthly tenant. After the death of Rajani Kanta the appellant did not pay any rent and though the heirs of Rajani Kanta served a notice under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act he refused to vacate the premises. Hence the suit for eviction was filed the defendant contested the suit on various grounds denying that he is a defaulter. It was contended that some of the heirs of Rajani Kanta namely Moneranjan Singha, Atomba Singha and Maya Debi left for India and the share of these persons have become enemy property and vested in the Government and the Government granted settlement of two-fifth share of the suit premises in V.P. Case No. 6176 and he paid rent to the Assistant Custodian, Enemy Property and obtained receipt thereof. The defendant contended that the suit is bad for defect of parties and the complicated question of title is also involved which cannot be tried by the court of Small Causes. The defendant filed and application under section 28A of the S.C.C. Act before the District Judge for withdrawal of the suit from the Court of the S.C.C. Judge. The learned District Judge observed: 

 In this view of the matter the suit was transferred to a Civil Court. This order was challenged before the High Court Division in Civil Revison No. 1479 of 1979. The High Court Division noticed that the defendant was a tenant under RajaniKanta. The S.C.C. Suit was filed in 1979 The defendant claimed that he took settlement from the Enemy Property in Vested Case No. 6 of 1979 dated 11.4.77; so the lease was taken subsequent to the filling of the suit and then the learned Single Judge observed: 

 "In the facts and circumstances of the case I hold that the Small Cause court Judge can decide this question in this proceeding and the Small Cause Court Judge is competent to incidentally decide the question of title. From the pleading of the petitioner it is essentially a case of Small Cause Court nature and title being as incidental question, the Court of Small Cause Judge can decide this issue". 

 3. It has been mentioned above that the learned. District Judge while passing the order on the application under section 28A of the S.C.C. Act noticed certain peculiar features of the case namely, whether one of the sons of Rajani Kanta named Monoranjan predeceased his father, whether vesting of 115th property was legal and whether the lease of 1/5th share to the petitioner is legal and binding. These circumstances led the District Judge to come to the conclusion that the suit should be tried by a Civil Court as a title suit instead of S.C.C Suit. It is regrettable that we have not found any reason that has been given by the learned Single Judge in the judgment. The burden of decision has been quoted above where a final opinion was passed by the learned Single Judge that "the S.C.C. Judge can decide this question in this proceeding" and then passed an opinion that no complicated question of title is involved in this case. In this view of the matter the order of the District Judge was set aside. 

 4. When the District "Judge noticed some peculiar features of the case and complicated question of title in view of the settlement in the vested property Case No.6 it precisely called for judicial scrutiny whether such question could be decided in a S.C.C. Suit. 

 6. Thus the legislative scheme is evident that complicated question of title is to be avoided by a Court of Small Causes. Section 24 provides for an appeal only in certain cases namely when an order passed under clause (ff) or clause (b) of section 104 (1) C.P.C. Under these clauses an order for payment for compensatory costs in respect of false or vexatious claim etc. or an order imposing a fine or the arrest or detention in Civil Prison are passed. Such orders are appealable .Then section 25 provides for revision in the following terms; 

 "25e. Revision of decrees and orders of Courts of Small Causes The High Court, for the purpose of satisfying itself that a decree or order made in any case decided by a Court of Small Causes was according to law, may call for the case and pass such order with respect thereto as it thinks fit. 

 In the present case when the matter was pending before the S.C.C. Court the learned District Judge came to the view that such suit cannot be tried by S.C. Court and accordingly passed the order under section 28A. Be it noted that the learned District Judge at the beginning of his order mentioned. "This is an application under section 28A of S.C.C. Act," Section 28A is in the following terms: 

 7A. It is obvious that the High Court Division considered the revision under section 25, Mr. M. H. Khondker appearing for the appellant canvassed that an order under section 28A is not revise able under section 25, Small Causes Courts- Act Section 25 of Small Causes Courts Act gives the jurisdiction to the High Court Division "for the purpose of satisfying itself that a decree or the order made in any case decided by a Court of Small Causes was according to law". In this case no S.C.C. Judge passed any decree nor any order was made by such court nor any-case was decided by the S.C. Court. The order was that of District Judge and it was passed under s. 28A. Section 25 does not confer any revisions jurisdiction against such order, 

 8. The revisional jurisdiction expressly conferred by section 25 is attracted only in a case decided by a S.C. Court to satisfy whether the decree or order made by such Court was according to law. A Court exercises jurisdiction which is conferred by law it cannot invent jurisdiction or confer a jurisdiction which is not given expressly. The learned Single Judge missed this very point that revisional jurisdiction under section 25 S.C.C. Act does not confer power of revision of an order tinder section 28A. It must be remembered that the Small Cause Courts Act is a self-contained Act and there, is no scope for invoking a revisional jurisdiction by way of reference. Section 28A was inserted by the Provincial Small Causes Courts (Amendment) Ordinance, 1962.(Ordinance LI of 1962). The 'Legislative intendment will be clarified if section- 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure is considered in juxtaposition. This section confers a general power of transfer/withdrawal of suit or appeal and other proceeding at any stage on the application of a party or its own motion and the power of the High Court Division and the District Judge are concurrent, Sub-section (4) of section 24 is in the following terms: 

 9. Prior to the amendment in 1962 transfer of Small Causes suit could be made under sec. 24(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure and the law says the transferred court will be "deemed to be court of Small Causes" The effect was that the suit must be tried under the Small Causes Court procedure without any right of appeal although the transferred Court does not possess S.C.C. power inasmuch as by the deeming provision the transferred court would be Small Causes Court for the purpose of the suit. No revision lay from such order (vide Kesho Vs. Goyal and Company, AIR 1938 Lahore, 95). But the position was changed in 1962 and 28A(2) provides: "Where a suit is so withdrawn the District Court or the Court to which such suit is transferred shall try and dispose of the same as if such suits were not cognizable by a court of Small Causes". Thus the position was altered sharply. In section 24 C P.C. the transferred Court would be deemed to be court of Small Causes but under section 28A (2) when a suit is' so withdrawn the Court shall try and dispose of the same "as if such suits were not cognizable by a court of Small Causes.'. Thus the procedure is also altered and the procedures laid down in the Small Causes Courts Act are no longer applicable. This independent and new remedy provided for by section 28-A has not been made revisable under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act. It has been held in R.Vs. Judge of Essax County Court (1887) 18 Q.B.D. 704 that in the case of an Act which creates a new jurisdiction, a new procedure, new forums or new remedy the Procedure, forms or remedies there prescribed and no others must be followed until altered by subsequent Legislation. The reason is obvious: A revision has been provided by the Legislature namely under section 25 of the Small Causes Courts Act and there is no scope for revision in the exercise of jurisdiction conferred by any other law because the enactment is of a special nature', The learned Single Judge has passed his opinion, without giving any reason It is imperative the all judgments must contain the reasons for the decisions. Order 20 rule 4 C.P.C says that a judgment shaJ1 contain, amongst others, the decision thereon and the reasons for such decision" In this case we have the decision but no reason. The decision of the learned Single Judge must be set aside. An order under section 28A is not revisable under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act because the effect of an order under see 28A is to take out the case from She ambit of Small Causes Court Act since it cannot be "adequately" tried by such court.
